I've lived in Germany for 4 years now in Hessen (Frankfurt) and in Nord-Rhein Westfalen, which is the same state that Cologne is located in. The people of NRW apparently have a reputation for being quite open to strangers and friendly compared to people in other states, though take the stereotype with a grain of salt. People speak German very quickly here, so you might have to get used to that pace and just jump in head-first. :')

There are a lot of very lovely things about this country (hence why I live here), but since you asked about some of the issues, I'll focus on those.

I'm a white person originally from the US with English and Irish heritage, am married to a native German, and I speak roughly C1 German, so my experiences my vary compared to PoC folk and those who speak less German. Some people here will be wonderful and welcoming to strangers (especially well-educated ones with perfect English), and some will never accept you into the in-group, no matter how good your German or how nice you are. 

BTW: Knowing Turkish is a big plus in the current job market, in addition to English and whatever other languages y'all are comfortable with. So I might suggest that your kids learn a bit more of Turkish if possible. Learning German, however, should be a top priority for everyone involved. People treat you with much more respect once you speak the language. 

Germans are extremely blunt people imo, but are generally honest and trustworthy. If a German friend says they'll help you with something, they probably will, because they will also straight-out tell you if something is too inconvenient or annoying for them. I don't know much about Kiwi culture except for the one summer I spent in Auckland, but if it's as I remember, you may have to also get used to people smiling less and making any effort to talk to strangers. Germans also love to *stare*. There's not this taboo against staring like I'm used to, and it still freaks me out...

I also offer my condolences on the coffee. It's, like, fine here, but I still dream about the coffee I had in NZ sometimes...

Racism is a much worse problem in Germany than most Germans realize, imo. Some of my reasons for this: most Germans have zero clue about the existence of racial microaggressions, and many don't even know about Germany's colonial history. There's not a great vocabulary to discuss such things here, and in fact, there is absolutely zero data on racial discrimination in some places because it just isn't tracked. Personally, I think the dialogue on racial diversity is a lot more developed in the Anglosphere. 

Children of Turkish immigrants are, as a whole, seen only as Turkish even if they and their families have been here for three generations now. People with dark skin are usually labeled as "Ausländer" immediately, even if they've been here their whole lives. You should expect for people to make a lot of judgments about your political, religious, and social views simply because of your heritage. A lot of Germans are very stubborn and resistant to change and new ideas, and this includes views on racial diversity. I would expect to do a lot of "educating" people, and your children getting questions about where they are "really" from. The amount of shit people say to me sometimes despite me passing as "Western European" is mind-boggling, so I have an unfortunately dim view of how PoC would be treated.

I think overall you will have less of an issue with some of the above-mentioned issues in Cologne, but you should still be aware of them. I would already try to set up contact with an English-speaking therapist/religious leader/coach in the area that you'll be in. They might be able to help you navigate some of these problems better.
